the classical optical criterion is not the most relevant for the final image quality and that the optimal defocus is not the same for all three criteria.

(a) the classical optical criterion does not provide the optimal focus for a rotationally symmetric optical system, and (b) the optimal focus depends on the sensor noise, and on the optical and digital restoration stages.

the design of hybrid optical-digital systems, where we take advantage of the best features of optics, such as high resolution and high speed, while using the best features of digital signal processing, such as robustness to aberrations, and the ability to perform restoration.
the development of new metrics for the evaluation of optical systems, with applications to the design of hybrid optical-digital cameras.
the design and analysis of optical and hybrid optical-digital systems, with a special focus on the impact of optical defects on the image quality.

, in order to achieve a good performance in a hybrid optical-digital system, the defocus should be chosen to be as close as possible to the defocus that would be chosen by the digital restoration filter.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
optical metrics are not always optimal, and that the use of a digital metric is highly recommended.
, for a given optical system, the optimal defocus is the defocus which minimizes the mean square error on a digital image, after an optical-digital hybrid processing.
the classical optical criterion does not provide the optimal focus, and that a more complex criterion is required to obtain the best results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optical design of a hybrid optical-digital system should account for the digital stage, as well as the expected image quality at the sensor, and not only for the optical quality.
the classical optical criterion is not a reliable metric for the design of hybrid optical-digital systems.
the classical optical criterion is no longer valid in hybrid optical-digital systems.
